# Testing ML systems {#sec-ch-ops-testing}

> *"Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to
> show their absence!"* — Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1970 [@dijkstra1970, §3]

```{python}
#| echo: false
import opsbook as ob
ob.setup()
import json, sys, time, ast, re, subprocess, textwrap
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import joblib
from scipy.stats import norm, binom
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
PY = sys.executable
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain why tests are written while developing, distinguish **unit,
  integration, end-to-end, contract, regression** and **property-based**
  tests, and map the tests of an ML system onto the **data / model /
  infrastructure** categories of the ML Test Score;
- write and run tests with **pytest**: discovery, assertions, fixtures and
  their scopes, parametrisation, markers, temporary directories, coverage;
  test a FastAPI service's **contract**;
- use a **linter** and a **formatter** (Ruff), configure them in
  `pyproject.toml`, and check the two properties that make a formatter safe in
  CI: **idempotence** and **preservation of the program**;
- test a model's **behaviour** — minimum functionality, invariance and
  directional expectations — and write **statistical** quality tests whose
  false-failure rate and power are chosen, using the **Wilson** interval and
  a sample-size formula proved from the normal approximation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
Why tests belong to development; the kinds of tests; linting and formatting;
pytest in practice; testing a machine-learning model.
:::

## Why test, and which tests {#sec-ops-test-kinds}

### Tests as executable specifications

A test is a small program that runs a piece of the system on chosen inputs and
checks the outputs against an expectation. Tests do not prove correctness —
Dijkstra's point — but they make three things cheap that are otherwise
expensive: **finding** a defect close to the change that introduced it,
**changing** code without fear (a refactoring that keeps the tests green kept
the specified behaviour), and **documenting** the intended behaviour in a form
that cannot go stale, because it runs. Written *during* development, they also
shape the code: a function that is hard to test usually does too much.

The usual taxonomy, by the size of what is exercised:

| Kind | What it exercises | Speed | Example in a sentiment service |
|---|---|---|---|
| **unit** | one function or class, in isolation | ms | the text normaliser maps `@someone` to `@user` |
| **integration** | several components together | ms–s | the service loads the model file and answers a request |
| **end-to-end / system** | the deployed system, from outside | s–min | `curl` on the running container returns a label |
| **contract** | the interface others rely on | ms | the request schema and response fields do not change by accident |
| **regression** | a bug that once happened | any | the empty string that crashed version 1.2 is rejected |
| **smoke** | "does it start at all" after a deploy | s | `/ready` returns 200 |
| **property-based** | a property over many generated inputs | s | normalising twice equals normalising once |

The **test pyramid** recommends many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests
and few slow end-to-end tests [@cohn2009, ch. 16], because the cost of
running and maintaining a test grows with what it touches, while its ability
to pinpoint a defect shrinks.

### Tests of an ML system

An ML system has two more things to test than ordinary software — the data
and the trained model — and its code includes training pipelines as well as
services. The ML Test Score (@def-ops-mltestscore) organises the tests in four
sections [@breck2017]:

- **data**: schemas and expectations on features, the cost and value of each
  feature, privacy controls, tests for the code that produces inputs;
- **model**: specifications reviewed and versioned, offline metrics that
  correlate with online impact, hyperparameters tuned, comparison with a
  simple baseline, quality on important slices, tests for fairness;
- **infrastructure**: reproducible training, unit tests for model code, an
  integration test of the whole pipeline, model quality validated before
  serving, debuggability, canary releases, rollback;
- **monitoring**: dependency changes, training–serving skew, staleness,
  numerical stability, performance (latency, throughput, memory), prediction
  quality.

This chapter writes tests of the first three kinds for the local model and
the service of @sec-ch-ops-serving; monitoring is @sec-ch-ops-monitor.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops4-kinds-easy}
## Easy — classify the tests
Classify each test by kind (unit, integration, end-to-end, contract,
regression, smoke, property-based) **and** by ML Test Score section (data,
model, infrastructure, monitoring): (a) the training data contain no posts
longer than 280 characters; (b) the model's accuracy on a fixed test set is at
least that of a majority-class baseline plus 30 points; (c) `POST /v1/predict`
with 65 texts returns 422; (d) retraining twice with the same inputs gives
identical model files; (e) for 1 000 random strings, the normaliser never
returns a longer string; (f) the model trained by the pipeline can be loaded
by the service image.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
The two classifications are independent: "kind" is about the size and style
of the test, "section" about what the test protects.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) A **data** test — a schema/expectation check, run as a unit-sized test on
the dataset. (b) A **model** test (comparison with a simple baseline), an
integration-sized test (data + training + evaluation). (c) A **contract**
test of the service — **infrastructure** in the rubric's terms (the serving
system). (d) An **infrastructure** test of reproducible training
(@exr-ops2-envs-hard); integration-sized. (e) A **property-based** unit test
of data-processing code (**data** section: tests for the code that produces
inputs). (f) An **integration** test across the pipeline and the serving
image (**infrastructure**: model validated before serving) — it catches,
for instance, a scikit-learn version mismatch between training and serving.
A common confusion is to call (b) a unit test because it is one `assert`.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-kinds-medium}
## Medium — unit tests for a normaliser
Social-media posts are usually normalised before a model sees them: user
mentions replaced by a placeholder, links by another, white space collapsed.
Write `normalise(text)` that maps every `@handle` to `@user`, every
`http(s)://…` link to `http`, collapses runs of white space and strips the
ends — and unit tests for it covering normal cases and edge cases (empty
string, only spaces, a mention at the end, an e-mail address, punctuation
attached to a link). Run them with pytest.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Decide first what *should* happen to `alice@example.org` — a mention or not?
Write that decision down as a test. `pytest.mark.parametrize` turns a table of
(input, expected) pairs into one test per row.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
norm_dir = ob.project("normaliser")
ob.write("textnorm.py", r'''
    """Normalisation of social-media posts before classification."""
    import re

    _MENTION = re.compile(r"(?<![\w.])@\w+")      # not preceded by a word character: excludes e-mails
    _LINK = re.compile(r"https?://\S+?(?=[)\].,!?;:]*(?:\s|$))")
    _SPACE = re.compile(r"\s+")


    def normalise(text: str) -> str:
        text = _MENTION.sub("@user", text)
        text = _LINK.sub("http", text)
        return _SPACE.sub(" ", text).strip()
''', base=norm_dir)
ob.write("tests/test_textnorm.py", r'''
    import pytest
    from textnorm import normalise


    @pytest.mark.parametrize("raw, expected", [
        ("love it @acme_support", "love it @user"),
        ("@a @b thanks", "@user @user thanks"),
        ("see https://example.org/x?y=1 now", "see http now"),
        ("link (https://example.org/a).", "link (http)."),
        ("write to alice@example.org", "write to alice@example.org"),   # e-mail: not a mention
        ("  too   many\tspaces \n", "too many spaces"),
        ("", ""),
        ("   ", ""),
    ])
    def test_normalise(raw, expected):
        assert normalise(raw) == expected


    def test_unicode_is_kept():
        assert normalise("perfetto 😍") == "perfetto 😍"
''', base=norm_dir)
ob.write("pyproject.toml", '[tool.pytest.ini_options]\npythonpath = ["."]\n', base=norm_dir)
ob.show("textnorm.py", base=norm_dir)
ob.show("tests/test_textnorm.py", base=norm_dir)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m pytest -q", cwd=norm_dir, shown="python -m pytest -q")
```
The table of cases *is* the specification; the e-mail case records a decision
(a lookbehind keeps `alice@example.org` intact) that a later edit of the
regular expression could silently reverse. The trailing punctuation case
shows why links need care: `\S+` alone would swallow `).` and change the
text around the link. A typical mistake is to test only the happy path; the
empty string and all-whitespace input are exactly what the service's
validation must also handle (@exr-ops3-fastapi-easy).
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-kinds-hard}
## Hard — properties instead of examples
Example-based tests check the cases you thought of. With the **Hypothesis**
library, state properties of `normalise` that must hold for *every* string —
idempotence (normalising twice changes nothing), no leading or trailing white
space, no double spaces, no `@` followed by a word character except `@user` — and let
Hypothesis search for counterexamples. Report any property that fails and fix
either the code or the property.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`@given(st.text())` generates arbitrary Unicode, including characters that
`\s` treats as white space and `str.strip()` does not, or the other way
round. When a property fails, Hypothesis *shrinks* the input to a minimal
counterexample: read it carefully.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ob.write("tests/test_properties.py", r'''
    import re
    from hypothesis import given, settings, strategies as st
    from textnorm import normalise

    # posts: sequences of arbitrary characters and of tricky fragments (mentions, links, spaces)
    pieces = st.characters(min_codepoint=0x20, max_codepoint=0x2FFF) | st.sampled_from(
        ["@", "@bob", "http://x.io/a", "https://e.org", " ", "\t", "\n", ".", ")", "\u00a0"])
    posts = st.lists(pieces, max_size=30).map("".join)


    @settings(max_examples=500, deadline=None)
    @given(posts)
    def test_idempotent(text):
        once = normalise(text)
        assert normalise(once) == once


    @settings(max_examples=500, deadline=None)
    @given(posts)
    def test_spacing(text):
        out = normalise(text)
        assert out == out.strip() and "  " not in out


    @settings(max_examples=500, deadline=None)
    @given(posts)
    def test_no_handles_left(text):
        assert all(h == "@user" for h in re.findall(r"(?<![\w.])@\w+", normalise(text)))
''', base=norm_dir)
ob.show("tests/test_properties.py", base=norm_dir)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/test_properties.py", cwd=norm_dir,
      shown="python -m pytest -q tests/test_properties.py",
      filt=lambda s: "\n".join(l for l in s.splitlines() if not l.startswith("  File")))
```
```{python}
#| echo: false
PROP_OK = ob.LAST.returncode == 0
```
Hypothesis ran 500 generated posts per property. `{python} "All three properties held" if PROP_OK else "At least one property failed, and Hypothesis printed a minimal counterexample above"`,
including idempotence: replacing a mention by `@user` produces a mention that
maps to itself, and a link by `http`, which is not a link any more — a fixed
point by design. Writing the properties forced a precise decision on what a
"handle" is (the same regular expression as the code — a property test that
copies the implementation tests little; here it is acceptable because the
property is about the *output* containing no other handles). Typical
counterexamples found by such tests in practice: non-breaking spaces, which
`\s` matches but a hand-written `" "` does not; a handle immediately after
a link; Unicode letters in handles.
:::

## pytest in practice {#sec-ops-pytest}

### The mechanics

**pytest** collects tests by convention: files named `test_*.py` (or
`*_test.py`), functions named `test_*`, classes named `Test*` [@pytest2026].
A test passes if it returns without raising; a plain `assert` is enough,
because pytest **rewrites** assertions at import time so that a failure
reports the values of both sides. Four features carry most of the work:

- **fixtures** — functions decorated with `@pytest.fixture` that build
  something a test needs (a model, a client, a temporary directory); a test
  asks for one by naming it as a parameter. The **scope** (`function`,
  `module`, `session`) says how often it is rebuilt; code after a `yield` in
  the fixture is the teardown. Fixtures shared by several files go in
  `conftest.py`;
- **parametrisation** — `@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs one test function on
  a table of inputs, each row reported separately;
- **markers** — labels such as `@pytest.mark.slow` select or skip groups of
  tests (`-m "not slow"`);
- **built-in fixtures** — `tmp_path` (a fresh directory), `monkeypatch`
  (set environment variables or attributes for one test), `capsys`, and more.

### A test suite for the service

Here is the service of @sec-ch-ops-serving with a test suite: a
session-scoped fixture starts the application **once** (loading the model is
the expensive part, @prp-ops-load-once), contract tests check the schema and
the error codes, and a few tests check that the answers make sense.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
train = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=1)
model = ob.train_model(train.text, train.label)
proj = ob.make_service(ob.project("svc_tests"), model)
ob.write("pyproject.toml", """
    [tool.pytest.ini_options]
    pythonpath = ["."]
    markers = ["slow: tests that train or evaluate a model"]
""", base=proj)
ob.write("tests/conftest.py", '''
    import os
    from pathlib import Path

    import pytest
    from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

    ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
    def client():
        """One application (and one model load) for the whole test session."""
        os.environ["MODEL_PATH"] = str(ROOT / "model.joblib")
        os.environ["MODEL_VERSION"] = "test"
        from app import app
        with TestClient(app) as c:      # entering runs the lifespan: the model is loaded here
            yield c
''', base=proj)
ob.write("tests/test_api.py", '''
    import pytest

    LABELS = {"negative", "neutral", "positive"}


    def test_health_and_ready(client):
        assert client.get("/health").json() == {"status": "ok"}
        assert client.get("/ready").json()["model_version"] == "test"


    def test_predict_shape(client):
        texts = ["the battery is awful", "got the camera today", "love the new phone"]
        r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"texts": texts})
        assert r.status_code == 200
        body = r.json()
        assert body["model_version"] == "test"
        assert len(body["predictions"]) == len(texts)
        for p in body["predictions"]:
            assert p["label"] in LABELS
            assert set(p["probabilities"]) == LABELS
            assert abs(sum(p["probabilities"].values()) - 1) < 1e-3
            assert p["label"] == max(p["probabilities"], key=p["probabilities"].get)


    @pytest.mark.parametrize("body", [
        {"texts": []},
        {"texts": [""]},
        {"texts": ["   "]},
        {"texts": ["x" * 281]},
        {"texts": ["ok"] * 65},
        {"texts": "not a list"},
        {"wrong": ["field"]},
    ])
    def test_invalid_requests_are_rejected(client, body):
        assert client.post("/v1/predict", json=body).status_code == 422


    def test_contract_of_request_schema(client):
        schema = client.get("/openapi.json").json()["components"]["schemas"]["PredictRequest"]
        texts = schema["properties"]["texts"]
        assert (texts["minItems"], texts["maxItems"]) == (1, 64)
        assert (texts["items"]["minLength"], texts["items"]["maxLength"]) == (1, 280)


    @pytest.mark.parametrize("text, expected", [
        ("love the new phone, brilliant camera", "positive"),
        ("the battery is awful and the app crashes", "negative"),
    ])
    def test_clear_cases(client, text, expected):
        r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"texts": [text]})
        assert r.json()["predictions"][0]["label"] == expected
''', base=proj)
ob.show("tests/conftest.py", base=proj)
ob.show("tests/test_api.py", base=proj)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m pytest -q --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing", cwd=proj,
      shown="python -m pytest -q --cov=app --cov-report=term-missing")
```

Twelve test cases from five test functions, one model load. The coverage
report — produced by `coverage.py` through the `pytest-cov` plug-in — lists
the lines of `app.py` that no test executed: typically the readiness error
branch, which needs a test that starts the application *without* a model.
Coverage measures what was **run**, not what was **checked**; 100 % coverage
with weak assertions proves little, and a low coverage points at untested
code.

When a test fails, assertion rewriting shows the values involved:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
ob.write("tests/test_failing.py", '''
    def test_label_of_negation(client):
        r = client.post("/v1/predict", json={"texts": ["the delivery is not bad"]})
        assert r.json()["predictions"][0]["label"] == "positive"
''', base=proj)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m pytest -q tests/test_failing.py", cwd=proj, shown="python -m pytest -q tests/test_failing.py",
      filt=lambda s: "\n".join(l for l in s.splitlines() if l.strip() and not l.startswith("tests/conftest")),
      max_lines=30)
(proj / "tests/test_failing.py").unlink()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
NOT_BAD = ob.LAST.returncode == 0
```

`{python} "The test passes: the model reads 'not bad' as positive (the bigram is in its vocabulary)." if NOT_BAD else "The test fails, and the report shows the label actually returned: a model of words and word pairs does not always handle negation."`
Such behaviours are what the model tests of @sec-ops-model-tests examine
systematically.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops4-pytest-easy}
## Easy — read the report
Without running it, say how pytest reports each of these tests (passed,
failed, error, skipped) and how many test cases it collects:
```python
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def data():
    raise RuntimeError("database down")

def test_uses_data(data):
    assert data

@pytest.mark.parametrize("n", [1, 2, 3])
def test_small(n):
    assert n < 3

@pytest.mark.skip(reason="model not trained yet")
def test_model():
    assert False

def helper_test():
    assert False
```
Then run it to check.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
pytest distinguishes a failing **assertion** in a test (failed) from an
exception while **setting up** a fixture (error). Which functions does it
collect?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz = ob.project("quiz")
ob.write("test_quiz.py", '''
    import pytest

    @pytest.fixture
    def data():
        raise RuntimeError("database down")

    def test_uses_data(data):
        assert data

    @pytest.mark.parametrize("n", [1, 2, 3])
    def test_small(n):
        assert n < 3

    @pytest.mark.skip(reason="model not trained yet")
    def test_model():
        assert False

    def helper_test():
        assert False
''', base=quiz)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m pytest -q -rA -p no:cacheprovider test_quiz.py", cwd=quiz, shown="python -m pytest -q -rA test_quiz.py",
      filt=lambda s: "\n".join(l for l in s.splitlines() if re.match(r"(PASSED|FAILED|ERROR|SKIPPED|\d+ )", l)))
```
Five test cases are collected: `test_uses_data`, three cases of `test_small`
and `test_model`; `helper_test` does not start with `test`, so it is not a
test (a common way for a "test" to never run). `test_uses_data` is an
**error** (its fixture raised during setup — the test itself never ran);
`test_small[3]` **fails**; `test_small[1]` and `[2]` pass; `test_model` is
skipped. Distinguishing errors from failures matters in CI: an error usually
means broken infrastructure (no database, no model file), a failure a broken
behaviour.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-pytest-medium}
## Medium — what a fixture's scope costs
Make model loading artificially slow (sleep 0.5 s in the lifespan), then run
the service's test suite with the `client` fixture at `function`, `module`
and `session` scope. Measure the total time and explain the numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
With `function` scope the fixture — and the lifespan — runs once per test
case. Pass the scope through an environment variable read in `conftest.py` so
the same suite can run three ways.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
conf = (proj / "tests/conftest.py").read_text()
slow_app = ob.SERVICE_APP.replace('STATE["model"] = joblib.load(', 'time.sleep(0.5)\n    STATE["model"] = joblib.load(')
(proj / "app.py").write_text(slow_app)
(proj / "tests/conftest.py").write_text(conf.replace('@pytest.fixture(scope="session")',
                                                     '@pytest.fixture(scope=os.environ.get("SCOPE", "session"))'))
for scope in ("function", "module", "session"):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    p = ob.run(f"{PY} -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider", cwd=proj, env={"SCOPE": scope})
    print(f"{scope:8s} {time.perf_counter() - t:5.1f} s  {p.stdout.strip().splitlines()[-1]}")
(proj / "app.py").write_text(ob.SERVICE_APP)            # restore
(proj / "tests/conftest.py").write_text(conf)
```
With `function` scope the model is loaded for each of the test cases, so the
suite takes several seconds of pure loading; with `module` or `session`
scope (one test module here) it is loaded once. The price of a broad scope is
shared state: a test that mutates the application (adds a route, changes a
global) affects the following ones — keep shared fixtures read-only.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-pytest-hard}
## Hard — catch a breaking change of the contract
Clients depend on the OpenAPI document. Write a test that compares the
current document with a stored **snapshot** and classifies each difference as
**breaking** (a removed endpoint or response field, a new required request
field, tighter limits) or **non-breaking** (a new endpoint, a new optional
field, looser limits), failing only on breaking ones. Demonstrate it on two
modified versions of the service: one that lowers the maximum text length
to 200, one that adds an optional `language` field.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Compare dictionaries recursively, but interpret only what clients depend on:
paths and methods, the request schema's `required` list and constraints
(`maxLength`, `maxItems` lower = breaking), and the response schema's
properties (removed = breaking).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
import importlib

def openapi_of(source: str) -> dict:
    mod_dir = ob.project("contract_mod")
    (mod_dir / "app_variant.py").write_text(source)
    sys.path.insert(0, str(mod_dir))
    sys.modules.pop("app_variant", None)
    mod = importlib.import_module("app_variant")
    sys.path.remove(str(mod_dir))
    return mod.app.openapi()

def breaking_changes(old: dict, new: dict) -> list[str]:
    issues = []
    for path, methods in old["paths"].items():
        for m in methods:
            if m not in new["paths"].get(path, {}):
                issues.append(f"removed {m.upper()} {path}")
    o_s, n_s = old["components"]["schemas"], new["components"]["schemas"]
    for name, schema in o_s.items():
        if name not in n_s:
            continue
        new_required = set(n_s[name].get("required", [])) - set(schema.get("required", []))
        issues += [f"{name}: new required field {f!r}" for f in new_required]
        for field, spec in schema.get("properties", {}).items():
            if field not in n_s[name].get("properties", {}):
                issues.append(f"{name}: removed field {field!r}")
                continue
            nspec = n_s[name]["properties"][field]
            for key in ("maxLength", "maxItems"):           # tighter upper limits break clients
                for a, b in ((spec, nspec), (spec.get("items", {}), nspec.get("items", {}))):
                    if key in a and b.get(key, np.inf) < a[key]:
                        issues.append(f"{name}.{field}: {key} {a[key]} -> {b[key]}")
    return issues

snapshot = openapi_of(ob.SERVICE_APP)
tighter = ob.SERVICE_APP.replace("max_length=280", "max_length=200")
optional = ob.SERVICE_APP.replace("texts: list[Text] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)",
                                  "texts: list[Text] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)\n    language: str | None = None")
print("tighter limit :", breaking_changes(snapshot, openapi_of(tighter)))
print("optional field:", breaking_changes(snapshot, openapi_of(optional)))
```
The lowered limit is reported as breaking (requests that were valid are now
rejected); the optional field is not (old requests remain valid). In a real
suite the snapshot is a JSON file committed next to the tests, updated
deliberately — together with a new API version — when a breaking change is
intended. Comparing the documents textually would fail on every harmless
reordering; the classification encodes *who* is affected by a change.
:::

## Linting and formatting {#sec-ops-lint}

### Linters

A **linter** analyses source code without running it and reports likely
errors and violations of conventions: a name used but never defined (a
`NameError` waiting for the branch that reaches it), an import never used, a
mutable default argument shared between calls, `== None` instead of `is None`,
a bare `except:` that swallows `KeyboardInterrupt`. **Ruff** implements the
rules of many older tools (Pyflakes, pycodestyle, isort, flake8 plug-ins such
as bugbear) in one fast program, configured in `pyproject.toml`
[@ruff2026]:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
lint = ob.project("lint")
ob.write("pyproject.toml", """
    [tool.ruff]
    line-length = 100

    [tool.ruff.lint]
    select = ["E", "F", "W", "I", "B", "UP"]   # pycodestyle, Pyflakes, warnings, isort, bugbear, pyupgrade
""", base=lint)
messy = '''import os, json
import numpy as np
from typing import List

def predict_all(texts: List[str], cache = {}):
    results=[]
    for t in texts:
        if cache.get(t) == None:
            cache[t] = model.predict([t])[0]
        results.append(cache[t])
    try:
        json.dumps(results)
    except:
        pass
    return results
'''
(lint / "service_utils.py").write_text(messy)
ob.show("service_utils.py", base=lint)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m ruff check --output-format concise .", cwd=lint, shown="ruff check --output-format concise .")
```

Each message names a rule: `F821` is a real bug (`model` is undefined), `B006`
a subtle one (the default `cache` dictionary is created once and shared by
every call — sometimes intended as a cache, usually a bug), `E722` a risky
habit, `F401` and `I001` hygiene. Some rules have automatic fixes
(`ruff check --fix`).

### Formatters, idempotence and safety

A **formatter** rewrites code into a canonical layout — line breaks,
indentation, quotes, spacing — so that layout is never discussed in review and
diffs show only meaningful changes. `ruff format` follows the style of Black
[@black2026]. Two properties make a formatter safe to run automatically:

::: {#prp-ops-formatter}
## What makes `format --check` meaningful
Let $F$ map source texts to source texts. (i) If $F$ is **idempotent**
($F \circ F = F$, @def-api-idempotent), then after formatting, a check that
compares $x$ with $F(x)$ always passes, and two developers who format the same
code get the same text whatever its previous layout, provided they started
from layouts with the same image under $F$. (ii) If $F$ **preserves the
abstract syntax tree** ($\mathrm{AST}(F(x)) = \mathrm{AST}(x)$, up to
docstring indentation), the formatted program means the same as the original.
:::

*In one line:* idempotence makes "is this file formatted?" a yes/no question
with a stable answer; AST preservation makes answering it harmless.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-formatter
(i) After formatting, the file is $y = F(x)$; the check compares $y$ with
$F(y) = F(F(x)) = F(x) = y$, so it passes. Two developers with inputs $x_1,
x_2$ and $F(x_1) = F(x_2)$ obviously agree after one pass; idempotence
guarantees that further passes (for instance by CI) do not move them apart.
Without it, a check could fail on code just formatted, and formatting in a
loop could oscillate. (ii) Python's semantics are defined on the parse tree:
two sources with the same AST compile to the same code objects (line numbers
aside), so they behave identically. Black and Ruff verify this property on
every file they format, by parsing before and after. $\blacksquare$
:::

Both properties can be checked directly:

```{python}
(lint / "service_utils.py").write_text(messy)
before_ast = ast.dump(ast.parse(messy))
ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format service_utils.py", cwd=lint, check=True)
once = (lint / "service_utils.py").read_text()
ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format service_utils.py", cwd=lint, check=True)
twice = (lint / "service_utils.py").read_text()
print(once)
print("idempotent:", once == twice, "| same AST as the original:", ast.dump(ast.parse(once)) == before_ast)
print("format --check exit code:", ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format --check service_utils.py", cwd=lint).returncode)
```

The formatter fixed the layout but not the bugs: `model` is still undefined
and the bare `except` is still there — formatting and linting are separate
jobs. In CI both run in **check** mode (non-zero exit code on any finding,
@sec-ch-ops-cicd); locally, a **pre-commit hook** runs them before each commit
so that problems never reach the repository [@precommit2026].

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops4-lint-easy}
## Easy — find the problems by hand
Without running a linter, list the problems in this function and the rule
families that would report them (Pyflakes, pycodestyle, bugbear, pyupgrade):
```python
from typing import Dict
import numpy as np

def label_counts(labels, counts: Dict[str, int]={}):
    for l in labels:
        if l not in counts: counts[l] = 0
        counts[l] +=1
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return {k: v/totl for k, v in counts.items()}
```
Then run Ruff to check your list.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Look for: something imported and unused, a default that persists across
calls, a name that does not exist, a variable name easy to confuse with a
digit, two statements on one line, and an outdated typing form.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz2 = ob.project("lint_quiz")
(quiz2 / "pyproject.toml").write_text((lint / "pyproject.toml").read_text().replace('"UP"]', '"UP", "E741"]'))
ob.write("counts.py", '''
    from typing import Dict
    import numpy as np

    def label_counts(labels, counts: Dict[str, int]={}):
        for l in labels:
            if l not in counts: counts[l] = 0
            counts[l] +=1
        total = sum(counts.values())
        return {k: v/totl for k, v in counts.items()}
''', base=quiz2)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m ruff check --output-format concise .", cwd=quiz2, shown="ruff check --output-format concise .")
```
The real bugs: `totl` is undefined (F821) — the function raises
`NameError` on every call that reaches the return; the mutable default
`counts={}` (B006) accumulates counts **across calls**, so a second call
returns frequencies of both label lists; `total` is assigned and never used
(F841), a symptom of the typo. Hygiene: unused `numpy` (F401), `l` as a name
(E741: ambiguous with `1`), a statement after a colon (E701), `Dict` instead
of `dict` (UP006/UP035). Linters find the two real bugs instantly — tests
would find the first only if a test reached that line.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-lint-medium}
## Medium — fix, format, verify
Fix the function of the previous exercise so that Ruff reports nothing (with
the configuration above), format it, and verify idempotence and that the AST
of the formatted file equals that of your fixed version. Add a unit test that
would have caught the mutable-default bug.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
The test calls the function twice with different labels and checks that the
second result does not depend on the first call.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
fixed = '''from collections import Counter


def label_counts(labels):
    """Relative frequency of each label."""
    counts = Counter(labels)
    total = sum(counts.values())
    return {label: count / total for label, count in counts.items()}
'''
(quiz2 / "counts.py").write_text(fixed)
ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format counts.py", cwd=quiz2, check=True)
formatted = (quiz2 / "counts.py").read_text()
print("ruff check:", ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff check counts.py", cwd=quiz2).stdout.strip())
print("AST preserved:", ast.dump(ast.parse(fixed)) == ast.dump(ast.parse(formatted)),
      "| idempotent:", ob.run(f"{PY} -m ruff format --check counts.py", cwd=quiz2).returncode == 0)
ob.write("test_counts.py", '''
    from counts import label_counts

    def test_calls_are_independent():
        assert label_counts(["a", "a", "b"]) == {"a": 2 / 3, "b": 1 / 3}
        assert label_counts(["c"]) == {"c": 1.0}     # the old version returned a, b and c
''', base=quiz2)
print(ob.run(f"{PY} -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider test_counts.py", cwd=quiz2).stdout.strip().splitlines()[-1])
```
`Counter` removes the hand-written counting and the shared default together.
The test encodes the property the bug violated — independence of calls —
rather than the implementation. A common half-fix is `counts=None` followed by
`counts = counts or {}`, which is correct here but hides the same bug if a
caller ever passes the dictionary on purpose.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-lint-hard}
## Hard — a quality gate in one command
Set up a small project with `pyproject.toml` (Ruff rules, line length, pytest
options), a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` with Ruff's hooks, and a script
`check.sh` that runs, in order, `ruff format --check`, `ruff check` and
`pytest`, and exits with the first non-zero status. Show that it fails on an
unformatted file, then on a lint error, then on a failing test, and passes
when all are fixed. Why this order?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`set -e` makes a Bash script stop at the first failing command. Order the
checks from the cheapest and most frequent failure to the most expensive —
@sec-ch-ops-cicd proves why this order minimises the expected cost.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
gate = ob.project("gate")
ob.write("pyproject.toml", """
    [tool.ruff]
    line-length = 100
    [tool.ruff.lint]
    select = ["E", "F", "W", "I", "B", "UP"]
    [tool.pytest.ini_options]
    pythonpath = ["."]
    addopts = "-q -p no:cacheprovider"
""", base=gate)
ob.write(".pre-commit-config.yaml", """
    repos:
      - repo: https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit
        rev: v0.17.5
        hooks:
          - id: ruff-check
            args: [--fix]
          - id: ruff-format
""", base=gate)
ob.write("check.sh", f"""
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    {PY} -m ruff format --check .
    {PY} -m ruff check .
    {PY} -m pytest
""", base=gate)
good_code = "def mean(xs):\n    return sum(xs) / len(xs)\n"
good_test = "from stats import mean\n\n\ndef test_mean():\n    assert mean([1, 2, 3]) == 2\n"
variants = {
    "unformatted": ("def mean(xs):  return sum(xs)/len(xs)\n", good_test),
    "lint error": ("import os\n\n\ndef mean(xs):\n    return sum(xs) / len(xs)\n", good_test),
    "failing test": ("def mean(xs):\n    return sum(xs) / (len(xs) + 1)\n", good_test),
    "all fixed": (good_code, good_test),
}
for name, (code, test) in variants.items():
    (gate / "stats.py").write_text(code)
    (gate / "test_stats.py").write_text(test)
    p = ob.run("bash check.sh", cwd=gate)
    last = ob.mask((p.stdout + p.stderr).strip().splitlines()[-1]) if p.returncode else "all checks passed"
    print(f"{name:13s} exit {p.returncode}: {last}")
```
Each variant stops at its first failing check. The order — format, lint,
tests — runs the cheapest checks first: they take milliseconds, fail often,
and a failure there makes the slower stages pointless. The pre-commit file
pins the hooks' version (`rev`) like any other dependency; installing it
(`pre-commit install`) runs the same checks before every commit. The same
three commands become the first job of the CI pipeline in @sec-ch-ops-cicd.
:::

## Testing the model {#sec-ops-model-tests}

### Behaviour, not just accuracy

A single accuracy number hides *which* inputs fail. Ribeiro et al. proposed
testing NLP models the way software is tested — with suites of targeted
cases organised by **capability** (vocabulary, negation, robustness to typos
or names…) and by **test type** [@ribeiro2020]:

- **minimum functionality tests (MFT)**: simple cases with a known answer
  ("the battery is awful" is negative), like unit tests;
- **invariance tests (INV)**: a perturbation that should **not** change the
  prediction — replacing one product with another, adding a neutral word,
  changing an emoji's skin tone;
- **directional expectation tests (DIR)**: a perturbation that should change
  the prediction **in a known direction** — adding "not" before a positive
  word should lower the probability of "positive"; appending "and the support
  team is rude" should not raise it.

Each test type runs over many generated cases and reports a **failure rate**:
the capability of a model is a rate, not a pass/fail bit. Let us run one test
of each type on the local model:

```{python}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
probe = ob.make_posts(600, seed=31)

def p_class(texts, k):                       # probability of class k for each text
    return model.predict_proba(list(texts))[:, k]

# MFT: one polar word on a topic, no noise
mft = [(f"{t} is {w}", 2) for t in ob.TOPICS for w in ("excellent", "brilliant", "perfect")] + \
      [(f"{t} is {w}", 0) for t in ob.TOPICS for w in ("terrible", "useless", "awful")]
mft_fail = np.mean(model.predict([t for t, _ in mft]) != np.array([y for _, y in mft]))

# INV: swap the topic for another topic: the label should not change
def swap_topic(text):
    for t in ob.TOPICS:
        if t in text:
            others = [o for o in ob.TOPICS if o != t]
            return text.replace(t, others[rng.integers(len(others))])
    return text
inv_src = [t for t in probe.text if any(tp in t for tp in ob.TOPICS)]
inv_fail = np.mean(model.predict(inv_src) != model.predict([swap_topic(t) for t in inv_src]))

# DIR: insert "not" before the first positive word: P(positive) must not increase
pos_posts = [t for t in probe.text if any(f" {w}" in f" {t}" for w in ob.POS) and " not " not in f" {t} "]
def negate(text):
    for w in ob.POS:
        if re.search(rf"\b{w}\b", text):
            return re.sub(rf"\b{w}\b", f"not {w}", text, count=1)
    return text
dir_fail = np.mean(p_class([negate(t) for t in pos_posts], 2) > p_class(pos_posts, 2) + 1e-9)

for name, rate, n in (("MFT clear polar posts", mft_fail, len(mft)),
                      ("INV swap the topic", inv_fail, len(inv_src)),
                      ("DIR insert 'not' before a positive word", dir_fail, len(pos_posts))):
    print(f"{name:42s} failure rate {rate:6.1%} on {n} cases")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
DIR_PCT = f"{100 * dir_fail:.0f}"
```

Clear cases pass and topics do not matter, as one would hope; but inserting
"not" raises the probability of "positive" in `{python} DIR_PCT` % of the
posts that contain a positive word — the model knows "not" only through the
word pairs it has seen. That is a finding no accuracy number would show,
and a regression test for the next version.

### Statistical tests of quality

"The accuracy on the test set is at least $\theta$" looks like a test, but
the accuracy measured on $n$ examples is a random variable: a good model can
fail it by bad luck, and a worse model can pass it. Two numbers make such a
test meaningful: its **false-failure rate** $\alpha$ (it fails although the
true accuracy is at the required level $p_0$) and its **power** $1 - \beta$
(it fails when the true accuracy has dropped to $p_1 < p_0$). Part III gave
Hoeffding's bound for the width of the estimate (@thm-test-set-size); here we
need something sharper.

::: {#prp-ops-wilson}
## Wilson's score interval
Let $\hat p = X/n$ with $X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n, p)$, and $z =
z_{1-\alpha/2}$ the standard normal quantile. The set of $p$ for which the
normal-approximation test $|\hat p - p| \le z\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ accepts is the
interval
$$
\frac{\hat p + \frac{z^2}{2n} \pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1 - \hat p)}{n} +
\frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \frac{z^2}{n}} ,
$$ {#eq-ops-wilson}
whose coverage is approximately $1 - \alpha$ [@wilson1927].
:::

*In one line:* instead of plugging $\hat p$ into the standard error (the
textbook "Wald" interval, poor near 0 and 1), keep the unknown $p$ in it and
solve for the $p$ values that the data do not reject.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-wilson
By the central limit theorem $(\hat p - p)/\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ is approximately
standard normal, so $P\bigl((\hat p - p)^2 \le z^2 p(1-p)/n\bigr) \approx 1 -
\alpha$. The inequality is quadratic in $p$: $(1 + z^2/n)p^2 - (2\hat p +
z^2/n)p + \hat p^2 \le 0$. The leading coefficient is positive, so the
solutions form the interval between the two roots, which the quadratic
formula gives as
$$
p = \frac{(2\hat p + z^2/n) \pm \sqrt{(2\hat p + z^2/n)^2 - 4(1 +
z^2/n)\hat p^2}}{2(1 + z^2/n)} ,
$$
and the discriminant simplifies to $4z^2\bigl(\hat p(1-\hat p)/n +
z^2/(4n^2)\bigr)$, giving @eq-ops-wilson. The event "$p$ is in the interval"
is the event "the test accepts $p$", whose probability is $\approx 1 -
\alpha$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The same approximation sizes a test.

::: {#prp-ops-test-size}
## Size of a one-sided quality test
A test that fails when $\hat p < \theta$ has false-failure rate $\le \alpha$
at true accuracy $p_0$ and power $\ge 1 - \beta$ at $p_1 < p_0$ (normal
approximation) if
$$
n \ge \left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} + z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)}}{p_0 - p_1}\right)^2,
\qquad \theta = p_0 - z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}} .
$$ {#eq-ops-test-size}
:::

*In one line:* the threshold must sit $z_{1-\alpha}$ standard errors below
the good accuracy and $z_{1-\beta}$ standard errors above the bad one; that is
possible only when $n$ makes the two distributions far enough apart.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-test-size
Under $p_0$, $\hat p \approx \mathcal N(p_0, p_0(1-p_0)/n)$, so $P(\hat p <
\theta) = \Phi\bigl((\theta - p_0)/\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\bigr) = \alpha$ exactly
for the stated $\theta$. Under $p_1$, the power is $P(\hat p < \theta) =
\Phi\bigl((\theta - p_1)/\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)/n}\bigr) \ge 1 - \beta$ iff
$\theta - p_1 \ge z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)/n}$. Substituting $\theta$:
$p_0 - p_1 \ge \bigl(z_{1-\alpha}\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)} +
z_{1-\beta}\sqrt{p_1(1-p_1)}\bigr)/\sqrt n$, and squaring gives the bound on
$n$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Let us check both on the local model, whose accuracy we can estimate
precisely with a very large sample from the generator:

```{python}
def wilson(k, n, conf=0.95):
    z = norm.ppf(1 - (1 - conf) / 2)
    ph = k / n
    centre = (ph + z**2 / (2 * n)) / (1 + z**2 / n)
    half = z * np.sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / (1 + z**2 / n)
    return centre - half, centre + half

def test_size(p0, p1, alpha=0.01, beta=0.10):
    za, zb = norm.ppf(1 - alpha), norm.ppf(1 - beta)
    n = int(np.ceil(((za * np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0)) + zb * np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1))) / (p0 - p1)) ** 2))
    return n, p0 - za * np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)

big = ob.make_posts(50_000, seed=77)
p_true = accuracy_score(big.label, model.predict(big.text))
small = ob.make_posts(300, seed=78)
k = int(np.sum(model.predict(small.text) == small.label))
lo, hi = wilson(k, 300)
hw = np.sqrt(np.log(2 / 0.05) / (2 * 300))                     # Hoeffding half-width (@thm-test-set-size)
print(f"accuracy on 50 000 posts: {p_true:.4f}")
print(f"300 posts: {k} correct, Wilson 95% [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}], Hoeffding 95% [{k/300 - hw:.4f}, {k/300 + hw:.4f}]")
n_req, theta = test_size(p_true, p_true - 0.05)
print(f"to catch a 5-point drop with power 90% and false failures <= 1%: n = {n_req}, threshold {theta:.4f}")
```

Hoeffding's interval is distribution-free but more than twice as wide for an
accuracy near 0.93; Wilson's is the one to use for decisions. The required
$n$ is modest for a 5-point drop and grows like $1/\delta^2$ for a drop of
$\delta$ points: a 1-point drop needs about 25 times as many examples.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops4-model-easy}
## Easy — Wilson by hand
A model labels 184 of 200 evaluation posts correctly. Compute the 95 % Wilson
interval with the formula (z = 1.96) and compare it with the Wald interval
$\hat p \pm z\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}$. Can you claim, at this confidence,
that the accuracy is above 0.90?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$\hat p = 0.92$, $z^2/n = 0.0192$. The claim "above 0.90" holds if the whole
interval is above 0.90.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
k, n, z = 184, 200, 1.96
ph = k / n
print("Wilson:", [round(float(v), 4) for v in wilson(k, n)])
print("Wald:  ", [round(float(ph - z * np.sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n)), 4), round(float(ph + z * np.sqrt(ph * (1 - ph) / n)), 4)])
```
Wilson gives about $[0.874, 0.950]$, Wald $[0.882, 0.958]$ — Wilson is
shifted towards 0.5, where the binomial is less skewed. Either way the lower
end is below 0.90: 200 posts cannot establish an accuracy above 0.90 when the
estimate is 0.92. The mistake is to read $\hat p = 0.92 > 0.90$ as the claim.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-model-medium}
## Medium — invariance and direction as pytest tests
Turn the INV and DIR tests of this section into a pytest module for the local
model: generate the cases in fixtures, and make each test fail if the failure
rate exceeds a tolerance (2 % for INV, 5 % for DIR). Add a DIR test of your
own: appending "and the support team is rude" to a post must not increase its
probability of being positive. Run the module and report which tests fail.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Save the model with `joblib` where the tests can load it, in a session
fixture. Report the observed rate in the assertion message so that a failure
says *how much*.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
beh = ob.project("behaviour")
joblib.dump(model, beh / "model.joblib")
ob.write("test_behaviour.py", f'''
    import re
    import sys
    from pathlib import Path

    import joblib
    import numpy as np
    import pytest

    sys.path.insert(0, {str(Path.cwd())!r})
    import opsbook as ob

    POSITIVE = 2


    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
    def model():
        return joblib.load(Path(__file__).parent / "model.joblib")


    @pytest.fixture(scope="session")
    def posts():
        return list(ob.make_posts(600, seed=31).text)


    def rate(flags):
        return float(np.mean(flags))


    def test_inv_topic_swap(model, posts):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
        src = [p for p in posts if any(t in p for t in ob.TOPICS)]
        def swap(p):
            t = next(t for t in ob.TOPICS if t in p)
            others = [o for o in ob.TOPICS if o != t]
            return p.replace(t, others[rng.integers(len(others))])
        r = rate(model.predict(src) != model.predict([swap(p) for p in src]))
        assert r <= 0.02, f"label changed after swapping the topic in {{r:.1%}} of {{len(src)}} posts"


    def test_dir_negation(model, posts):
        src = [p for p in posts if any(re.search(rf"\\b{{w}}\\b", p) for w in ob.POS) and " not " not in f" {{p}} "]
        def negate(p):
            w = next(w for w in ob.POS if re.search(rf"\\b{{w}}\\b", p))
            return re.sub(rf"\\b{{w}}\\b", f"not {{w}}", p, count=1)
        before = model.predict_proba(src)[:, POSITIVE]
        after = model.predict_proba([negate(p) for p in src])[:, POSITIVE]
        r = rate(after > before + 1e-9)
        assert r <= 0.05, f"'not' raised P(positive) in {{r:.1%}} of {{len(src)}} posts"


    def test_dir_rude_suffix(model, posts):
        before = model.predict_proba(posts)[:, POSITIVE]
        after = model.predict_proba([p + " and the support team is rude" for p in posts])[:, POSITIVE]
        r = rate(after > before + 1e-9)
        assert r <= 0.05, f"a rude remark raised P(positive) in {{r:.1%}} of {{len(posts)}} posts"
''', base=beh)
ob.sh(f"{PY} -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider --tb=line test_behaviour.py", cwd=beh,
      shown="python -m pytest -q --tb=line test_behaviour.py",
      filt=lambda s: "\n".join(l for l in s.splitlines() if l.strip()))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_names = {"test_inv_topic_swap": "the topic swap", "test_dir_negation": "the negation test",
          "test_dir_rude_suffix": "the rude remark"}
_failed = [k for k in _names if f"test_behaviour.py::{k}" in ob.LAST.stdout]
BEH_SUMMARY = ("All three tests pass." if not _failed else
               "Failing: " + ", ".join(_names[k] for k in _failed) + "; passing: "
               + (", ".join(v for k, v in _names.items() if k not in _failed) or "none") + ".")
```
`{python} BEH_SUMMARY` A failing assertion says by how much the rate
exceeds its tolerance — the local model's weakness with negation shows up as a
number, not as an anecdote. Tolerances are part of the specification: a DIR
test that tolerates 0 % failures would block every model trained on noisy
labels; one that tolerates 50 % tests nothing. Behavioural suites are most
useful as **regression** tests between model versions: the rate may not get
worse.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-model-hard}
## Hard — a quality test with known error rates
Design an automated test "the model's accuracy has not dropped by 5 points or
more" with a false-failure rate of at most 1 % and a power of at least 90 %,
using @eq-ops-test-size. Then **check the error rates by simulation**: draw
2 000 evaluation sets of the required size for the current model, and 2 000
for a degraded model whose accuracy is 5 points lower (build it by flipping a
fraction of the current model's correct answers), and count how often the
test fails in each case. Repeat with half the required sample size.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Simulate the number of correct answers directly as binomial draws once you
know the two true accuracies — the model need not be re-run 4 000 times.
Compare the observed failure frequencies with $\alpha$ and $1 - \beta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
p0, p1 = p_true, p_true - 0.05
rng_sim = np.random.default_rng(5)
for n_eval in (n_req, n_req // 2):
    theta_n = p0 - norm.ppf(0.99) * np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n_eval)
    good = rng_sim.binomial(n_eval, p0, size=2000) / n_eval
    bad = rng_sim.binomial(n_eval, p1, size=2000) / n_eval
    print(f"n = {n_eval:4d}, threshold {theta_n:.4f}: false failures {np.mean(good < theta_n):.3f} (target 0.01), "
          f"power {np.mean(bad < theta_n):.3f} (target 0.90)")
```
With the size from @eq-ops-test-size the simulated false-failure rate is close
to 1 % and the power close to 90 % — the normal approximation is good at these
sizes. With half the examples, keeping $\alpha$ at 1 % forces the threshold
lower and the power falls to about two thirds: the test would let one 5-point
regression in three through. Note what the test needs to be *automated*: a fixed evaluation set
(or one sampled from a fixed pool), the reference accuracy $p_0$ measured with
far more data than the test uses, and the threshold computed, not chosen by
feel. @sec-ch-ops-cicd compares two models on the **same** examples, which
needs fewer of them.
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The project asks for tests of the API and of the model's
behaviour. For the API: a session-scoped client fixture (the transformer is
expensive to load), contract tests of the schema and status codes, rejection
of empty and too long inputs, labels always in the three expected classes,
probabilities summing to one (@sec-ops-pytest). For the model: a few clear
positive and negative examples as minimum-functionality tests, plus invariance
and directional tests whose tolerances are written down
(@exr-ops4-model-medium) — and, if a quality threshold is asserted, a sample
size and threshold computed for chosen error rates (@exr-ops4-model-hard).
Ruff in check mode and the tests make the first stage of the pipeline
(@exr-ops4-lint-hard).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Tests that never run**: names not starting with `test`, files outside
  discovery, skipped tests forgotten.
- **Function-scoped fixtures for expensive resources** — and session-scoped
  fixtures that tests mutate.
- **Coverage as a goal**: lines executed are not behaviours checked.
- **Formatting and linting confused**: the formatter fixes layout, not bugs.
- **Accuracy thresholds chosen by feel** on small evaluation sets: flaky
  tests or tests that cannot fail.
- **Behavioural tests with zero tolerance** on models trained on noisy labels.
- **Testing the model's training data**: evaluation examples must be unseen
  (@sec-leakage).
:::

## Summary

- Tests are executable specifications; the pyramid favours many fast unit
  tests. ML systems add data and model tests to the usual infrastructure
  tests (ML Test Score sections).
- pytest: discovery by name, rewritten assertions, fixtures with scopes and
  teardown, parametrisation, markers, `tmp_path`, coverage via `pytest-cov`.
  A FastAPI service is tested in-process with `TestClient`: schema, status
  codes, contract.
- Ruff lints (Pyflakes, pycodestyle, bugbear, isort, pyupgrade rules) and
  formats (Black style). A formatter is safe because it is idempotent and
  preserves the AST; CI runs both in check mode, pre-commit runs them before
  commits.
- Behavioural tests (MFT, INV, DIR) measure capabilities as failure rates.
  Quality tests are statistical: the Wilson interval
  @eq-ops-wilson estimates accuracy; @eq-ops-test-size sizes a test for a
  chosen false-failure rate and power.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ops4-slices}
**Accuracy by slice.** Compute the accuracy of the local model, with a Wilson
interval, on three slices of a large evaluation set: posts with a negation,
posts with an emoji, posts with more than ten words. Which slices are
significantly worse than the overall accuracy?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
ev = ob.make_posts(20_000, seed=90)
pred = model.predict(ev.text)
ok = pred == ev.label.to_numpy()
slices = {"all": np.ones(len(ev), bool),
          "negation": ev.text.str.contains(r"\bnot\b", regex=True).to_numpy(),
          "emoji": ev.text.str.contains(r"[^\w\s]", regex=True).to_numpy(),
          "more than ten words": (ev.text.str.split().str.len() > 10).to_numpy()}
for name, m in slices.items():
    lo, hi = wilson(ok[m].sum(), m.sum())
    print(f"{name:20s} n = {m.sum():5d}  accuracy {ok[m].mean():.4f}  95% [{lo:.4f}, {hi:.4f}]")
```
Negated posts are clearly worse — their interval lies entirely below the
overall accuracy; emojis help (they carry the sentiment in this generator).
Slice tests belong to the "model" section of the ML Test Score; the intervals
keep a small slice from being declared "worse" by noise.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-flaky}
**Flaky suites.** A suite has 40 independent statistical tests, each with a
false-failure rate of 1 %. What is the probability that a good model fails at
least one of them? What per-test rate keeps the suite's false-failure rate
below 1 %, and what does that cost in sample size for one test sized as in
@exr-ops4-model-hard?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
m_tests = 40
print(f"P(at least one false failure) = {1 - 0.99**m_tests:.3f}")
alpha_each = 0.01 / m_tests                     # Bonferroni: union bound
za_old, za_new, zb = norm.ppf(0.99), norm.ppf(1 - alpha_each), norm.ppf(0.90)
n_old = ((za_old * np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0)) + zb * np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1))) / (p0 - p1)) ** 2
n_new = ((za_new * np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0)) + zb * np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1))) / (p0 - p1)) ** 2
print(f"per-test rate {alpha_each:.5f}; sample size x{n_new / n_old:.2f}")
```
With 40 tests at 1 % each, a good model fails at least one a third of the
time — the suite is flaky by construction. By the union bound, a per-test rate
of $0.01/40$ keeps the suite below 1 % (Bonferroni's correction), at the cost
of about 1.7 times the sample size for each test. @sec-ch-ops-monitor meets the
same problem with drift tests run on many windows.
:::

::: {#exr-ops4-baseline}
**A baseline test.** Write a test that the local model beats a
majority-class baseline and a keyword baseline (positive if it contains a
word of `ob.POS`, negative if of `ob.NEG`, neutral otherwise) on the same
evaluation set, with a paired comparison. By how much does it beat each?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
def keyword(text):
    words = set(text.split())
    pos, neg = len(words & set(ob.POS)), len(words & set(ob.NEG))
    return 2 if pos > neg else 0 if neg > pos else 1

y_ev = ev.label.to_numpy()
majority = np.full(len(ev), np.bincount(train.label).argmax())
kw = np.array([keyword(t) for t in ev.text])
for name, b in (("majority", majority), ("keyword", kw)):
    win, loss = np.sum((pred == y_ev) & (b != y_ev)), np.sum((pred != y_ev) & (b == y_ev))
    print(f"vs {name:8s}: baseline accuracy {np.mean(b == y_ev):.4f}; model wins {win}, loses {loss} "
          f"-> difference {(win - loss) / len(ev):+.4f}")
```
The model beats the majority class by a wide margin and the keyword rule by a
smaller but large one (the rule fails on negations and mixed posts). Counting
wins and losses on the *same* examples is the basis of the paired test of
@sec-ch-ops-cicd; a model that cannot beat a keyword list does not deserve the
complexity of an ML pipeline — the "baseline" test of the ML Test Score.
:::
